extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic and philosophy (those learning to analyse or construct arguments and syllogisms)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analytic rules for distinguishing induction and ratiocination, for forming legitimate syllogisms (figures, modes, terms, conversion and reduction), and for understanding the logical axioms that ground syllogistic inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Induction and Ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is inferring a proposition from propositions less general than itself (ascending from particulars to generals or combining generals to more general propositions); Ratiocination (syllogism) is inferring a proposition from propositions equally or more general than itself (reasoning from generals to particulars or to less general propositions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the intended meaning: 'Induction is inferring a proposition from propositions less general than itself, and Ratiocination is inferring a proposition from propositions equally or more general.' The terms 'reasoning from particulars to generals' and 'from generals to particulars' are convenient but imprecise without commentary; classify arguments by comparing the generality of conclusion versus premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential structure of a legitimate syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate syllogism must have three, and no more than three, propositions (two premises and one conclusion) and exactly three terms: the major term (predicate of the conclusion), the minor term (subject of the conclusion), and the middle term (occurring in both premises to connect the other two).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the middle term appears in both premises and that each of major and minor appears in one premise only (with the middle). The premises should jointly prove the conclusion; if more/fewer propositions or terms occur, the argument is not a canonical syllogism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures of syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogisms are classified into figures (commonly three or four) according to the position of the middle term: (1) middle term subject of major and predicate of minor (first figure); (2) middle term predicate in both premises (second figure); (3) middle term subject in both (third figure); (4) middle term subject of minor and predicate of major (fourth figure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize which figure an argument naturally falls into; authors sometimes compress the fourth into the first. Choosing a figure can make the naturalness and immediacy of the argument clearer, though any valid argument can be transformed to the first figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes by quantity and quality (legitimate modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each figure is subdivided into modes according to the quantity (universal or particular) and quality (affirmative or negative) of the propositions. Only certain combinations (the listed modes) are legitimate — i.e., the conclusion correctly follows when premises are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to canonical exemplars (the text lists legitimate modes for all four figures with concrete forms such as 'All B is C; All A is B; therefore All A is C', and negative/particular alternatives). Use those exemplars as templates for constructing valid syllogisms; other arbitrary combinations will not guarantee validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of singular propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular propositions (e.g., 'Socrates is a man') are ranked with universal propositions for syllogistic purposes because their predicate is affirmed or denied of the whole of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fitting singulars into syllogisms, treat them as universals (they function as if asserting the predicate of an entire subject), so they can be slotted into the standard modes without special forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of syllogisms to the first figure
rubrics_metrics.description: All correct ratiocination admits of being stated in syllogisms of the first figure alone; syllogisms of the other figures can be converted (one or both premises) into equivalent premises making the argument first-figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply conversion rules (simple or per accidens) to change premises' expression while preserving truth so as to reframe the argument in the first figure. Reduction is useful to clarify validity and is standard practice in syllogistic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion rules for premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal negatives admit simple conversion (No C is B → No B is C). Universal affirmatives do not admit simple conversion but may be converted 'per accidens' into particulars (All B is A → Some A is B) which preserves a part of the original assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple conversion for universal negatives to change their order without loss; convert universal affirmatives only per accidens when reducing figures — doing so may weaken the scope (from universal to particular) but yields a premise that is true if the original is true. Examples in the text demonstrate both maneuvers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major and minor premise roles and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The major premise of a syllogism is always a universal proposition (affirmative or negative) and, together with the (always affirmative) minor premise, determines the conclusion's quality (affirmative/negative) and generality (more/less/equally general than premises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a syllogism, check that the major is universal, the minor affirmative, and that their combination legitimately supports the conclusion's form. The position and type of these premises shape whether the conclusion will be universal/particular and affirmative/negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity criterion for syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: A syllogism is legitimate when, if the premises are true, the conclusion must necessarily be true — i.e., the conclusion follows with necessity from the premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test validity by attempting reduction to canonical first-figure forms or by checking that the middle term properly connects subject and predicate according to legitimate modes. Validity is independent of the empirical truth of premises; it concerns the logical necessity of the inferential relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism as inference by marks (practical-epistemic formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recast syllogisms as: 'Attribute A is a mark of attribute B; a given object has mark A; therefore the object has attribute B.' That is, a general affirmative proposition functions as asserting that one attribute serves as a sign or evidence of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this 'mark' formulation when analysing syllogisms for their practical function (inference from signs). It clarifies ratiocination's role as an aid in practical judgment: premises act as evidential marks for attributes to be inferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental axioms grounding syllogistic inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Two principles are the ground of legitimate syllogistic inference (as facts, not conventions): (1) Affirmative axiom — things which coexist with the same thing coexist with one another. (2) Negative axiom — if a thing coexists with a second thing which does not coexist with a third, then the first does not coexist with the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending or testing syllogistic moves, appeal to these factual axioms rather than to the verbal dictum de omni et nullo. They express the real relations among attributes that make the inference informative rather than merely verbal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of dictum de omni et nullo as sole foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: The dictum 'whatever can be affirmed (or denied) of a class may be affirmed (or denied) of everything included in the class' is merely tautologous if classes are nothing but collections of individuals; it cannot serve alone as the foundation of ratiocination because real propositions assert matters of fact (coexistence or incompatibility of attributes) not mere class membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating syllogistic inference as pure manipulation of names/classes; instead evaluate premises for their factual content about attributes and natural laws. Recognize the risk of reducing reasoning to mere verbal substitution (the 'names-only' critique) and demand substantive factual import in premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions convey factual relations, not mere classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Every proposition conveying real information asserts a matter of fact about attributes (that a given object has or lacks an attribute, or that two attributes coexist or do not), rather than merely indicating class inclusion or word-meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or judging syllogisms, ensure premises commit to factual claims about attributes and their coexistence/incompatibility. Arguments that rest purely on classificatory conventions risk being 'solemn trifling' and not informative about the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical ordering advice when studying knowledge sources
rubrics_metrics.description: It can be advantageous, in tracing acquired knowledge to its sources, to begin with ratiocination (syllogism) and trace derivative truths backward to the truths from which they are deduced, before treating induction (the original spring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this methodological order when analysing the evidential dependence of claims: start with how conclusions follow from general principles (ratiocination), then examine how those general principles are themselves grounded (induction). This order can make the dependence relations clearer.
